column2: Papadopoulou, A.; Laucks, J.; Tibbits, S.
column4: From self-assemblies to evolutionary structures
column9: The Self‐Assembly Lab at Massachusetts Institute of Technology is at the forefront of the move towards evolutionary construction processes. Three of the Lab's members – doctoral researcher Athina Papadopoulou, co‐director Jared Laucks and co‐founder Skylar Tibbits – report on its recent experiments in macro‐scale fabrication that relies on the reactions of specially designed material components, both among themselves and with their environment.
column20: Assembly behaviour is encoded in material units and activated by supplied energy without an ongoing digital feedback loop. Local interactions permit autonomous organisation, but the system remains bounded and does not include wider contextual exchange, material return, or ecological replenishment.

column2: Raviv, D.; Zhao, W.; McKnelly, C.; Papadopoulou, A.; Kadambi, A.; Shi, B.; Hirsch, S.; Dikovsky, D.; Zyracki, M.; Olguin, C.; Raskar, R.; Tibbits, S.
column4: Active printed materials for complex self-evolving deformations
column9: We propose a new design of complex self-evolving structures that vary over time due to environmental interaction. In conventional 3D printing systems, materials are meant to be stable rather than active and fabricated models are designed and printed as static objects. Here, we introduce a novel approach for simulating and fabricating self-evolving structures that transform into a predetermined shape, changing property and function after fabrication. The new locally coordinated bending primitives combine into a single system, allowing for a global deformation which can stretch, fold and bend given environmental stimulus.
column20: Transformation is physically programmed during fabrication and triggered by water; no operational digital feedback loop updates the material. Target deformation and stimulus–response relations are predefined within the fabricated object, with no wider contextual or renewal mechanism.

column2: Tibbits, S.
column4: Fluid Crystallization: Hierarchical Self-Organization
column5: FABRICATE 2014: Negotiating Design & Making. F. Gramazio, M. Kohler and S. Langenberg, UCL Press
column9: New self-assembly technologies and programmable material possibilities are emerging across length-scales and disciplinary boundaries, offering shape-changing and intelligent biological, chemical, and material assemblies. This paper proposes the study of chemical interactions and material phase-change between crystalline solids, liquids and gases as a scalable approach for macro-scale assemblies of programmable materials. The Fluid Crystallisation project is highlighted as the first physical example of macro-scale self-organisation of non-deterministic and hierarchical structures. Offering a vision towards the future of fabrication and manufacturing, this project expands the palette of techniques outside of traditional additive or subtractive methodologies into fluid realms of programmable assembly and adaptive material behaviour.
column20: Self-organisation emerges from material interactions under supplied energy, but no explicit digital feedback loop operates during assembly. The experiment is bounded; local interactions create variable configurations while ecological exchange and renewal are not addressed.

column2: Cohen, Z., Elberfeld, N., Moorman, A., Laucks, J., Kernizan, S., Holmes, D. and Tibbits, S., 2020.
column4: Superjammed: Tunable and morphable spanning structures through granular jamming.
column9: This paper introduces a method of post-tensioning granular jammed structures to achieve horizontal spans that can be tuned and morphed, as well as withstand significant vertical loads. The paper begins by discussing recent research into jammed structures. The methods section details the development of the fabrication system that led to post-tensioned, jammed—or “superjammed”—structures. The ability to structurally tune, geometrically morph, and instantly reverse superjammed structures is discussed. The performative possibilities of superjammed structures are demonstrated through the prototyping of large-scale spanning typologies. The results of abrasion testing on a superjammed structure are also briefly presented. The outlook section summarizes the benefits of superjammed structures and outlines further research into their limitations, including load capacity, scalability, and weather resistance.
column20: Granular jamming enables reversible changes in form and stiffness through controlled confinement. Reconfiguration occurs within a bounded material platform without ongoing digital sensing or contextual exchange; reversibility supports limited reuse but not ecological renewal.

column4: Growing Islands
column9:
What if we could harness the power of the ocean to grow islands, rebuild beaches and protect coastal communities from sea level rise? 
MIT’s Self Assembly Lab and Invena, an organization based out of the Maldives, are working together to create a system of underwater structures that use wave energy to promote sand accumulation in strategic locations. Over time, the goal is that the self-organization of sand will grow into new islands or help rebuild coastlines, creating an adaptable solution to protect coastal communities from rising sea levels.
column20: Low-density structures operate in an open marine context where wave energy, sediment movement and vegetation contribute to continuing accretion and stabilisation. Digital feedback is not central, but contextual exchange, material accumulation and ecological renewal are explicit features of the system.

column5: ACADIA 2022: Hybrids and Haecceities [Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Conference of the Association of Computer Aided Design in Architecture (ACADIA) ISBN 979-8-9860805-8-1]. University of Pennsylvania Stuart Weitzman School of Design. 27-29 October 2022. edited by M. Akbarzadeh, D. Aviv, H. Jamelle, and R. Stuart-Smith.
column9: This paper discusses an ongoing interdisciplinary research project that develops a design and fabrication approach termed; tunable environments. This is an explorative approach, which enables updates from a digital parametric interface to be ‘pushed' into a 2D, 18 x 18 cm material sample, by modulating stimuli, so multiple properties can be updated/tuned at high resolutions. Our prototype explores how iterative updates can be achieved, which can be temporarily frozen in time. This opens up the idea of creating Parametric Matter/circular mate- rials, which could reduce waste that can be attributed to typical linear processes. Additionally, highly bespoke, ‘time-based’ structures could be achieved
column19: 2D material sample
column20: A digital interface repeatedly pushes parametric updates into a bounded magnetised-thermoplastic sample, but the material does not directly update the digital model. Lag and material legacy expose mismatches between predefined digital relationships and realised physical states.

column2: Blaney, A.
column4: Material Units - Uploading information into matter via stimuli and the challenges of determining feedback
column5: Stojakovic, V and Tepavcevic, B (eds.), Towards a new, configurable architecture - Proceedings of the 39th eCAADe Conference - Volume 2, University of Novi Sad, Novi Sad, Serbia, 8-10 September 2021, pp.
column9: Associative and generative design processes are capable of creating complex digital models, which can have their digital material properties (size, aesthetics, performance) infinitely adapted or radically transformed, relative to design demands, if they remain in their digital environments. Imagine, if physical materials and structures had these abilities, where design updates could be uploaded into a structure's physical material makeup at molecular resolutions. This could begin to enable a physical structure's matter to be reprogrammed so they can adapt across their length scales with high sensitivities and multi-material properties. To leverage these abilities, novel design and fabrication processes need to be developed, which enable interrelationships between design parameters, assembly mechanisms and material properties. This paper presents key findings and implications of two final prototypes, from a series, which developed a design and fabrication approach termed tuneable environments that enables interrelationships and design information to be uploaded into matter at granular resolutions.
column19: Material unit → material system
column20: Sensed changes and controlled dosing support material growth, while electrical changes provide indirect feedback about accretion. Digital–material discourse is therefore strong within a bounded laboratory system, although input–response associations remain only partly adaptive.

column2: Ayres, P. (ed.)
column4: Persistent Modelling: Extending the Role of Architectural Representation

column2: Hamann, H.; Divband Soorati, M.; Heinrich, M. K.; Hofstadler, D. N.; Kuksin, I.; Veenstra, F.; Wahby, M.; Nielsen, S. A.; Risi, S.; Skrzypczak, T.; Zahadat, P.; Wojtaszek, P.; Støy, K.; Schmickl, T.; Kernbach, S.; Ayres, P.
column4: Flora robotica — An Architectural System Combining Living Natural Plants and Distributed Robots
column5: Proceedings of ECAL 2017: 14th European Conference on Artificial Life
column9: Key to our project flora robotica is the idea of creating a bio-hybrid system of tightly coupled natural plants and distributed robots to grow architectural artifacts and spaces. Our motivation with this ground research project is to lay a principled foundation towards the design and implementation of living architectural systems that provide functionalities beyond those of orthodox building practice, such as selfrepair, material accumulation and self-organization. Plants and robots work together to create a living organism that is inhabited by human beings. User-defined design objectives help to steer the directional growth of the plants, but also the system’s interactions with its inhabitants determine locations where growth is prohibited or desired (e.g., partitions, windows, occupiable space). We report our plant species selection process and aspects of living architecture. A leitmotif of our project is the rich concept of braiding: braids are produced by robots from continuous material and serve as both scaffolds and initial architectural artifacts before plants take over and grow the desired architecture. We use light and hormones as attraction stimuli and far-red light as repelling stimulus to influence the plants. Applied sensors range from simple proximity sensing to detect the presence of plants to sophisticated sensing technology, such as electrophysiology and measurements of sap flow. We conclude by discussing our anticipated final demonstrator that integrates key features of flora robotica, such as the continuous growth process of architectural artifacts and self-repair of living architecture.
column19: Plant physiology → robotic nodes → architectural system / inhabitants
column20: Distributed sensing and robotic stimuli create explicit ongoing feedback with living plants. Plant growth is adaptive and history-dependent, but it is steered towards defined architectural objectives inside a designed bio-hybrid system; wider contextual exchange and renewal are present only partially.

column2: Ayres, P.
column4: Microstructure, macrostructure and the steering of material proclivities
column5: In Manufacturing the Bespoke: Making and Prototyping Architecture
column9: Ayres investigates free internal-pressure forming of steel as a materially non-deterministic fabrication process. Hydroforming exposes complex interactions between microstructural and macrostructural levels that produce irreversible material and performance transformations that can be steered but not completely prescribed through geometry. Because inflation can be arrested and resumed, Ayres proposes extending forming beyond a discrete fabrication phase and develops the Persistent Model as a circular digital–physical relationship in which the physical artefact re-informs its representation through feedback over time.
column19: atomic lattice → grain → component → aggregate → representation
column20: Persistent Model #1 links physical pressure and realised material behaviour back to the representation through error-regulated feedback. Material behaviour is nonlinear and history-dependent, but the implemented system remains bounded to the hydroformed assembly and does not include wider ecological exchange or renewal.

column2: Correa, D.; Papadopoulou, A.; Guberan, C.; Jhaveri, N.; Reichert, S.; Menges, A.; Tibbits, S.

column20: Digital fabrication programs hygroscopic transformation into anisotropic multimaterial structures, after which environmental moisture triggers the response autonomously. column19: Bacteria + fluid/material conditions → mineral deposition → structure
column20: No live digital feedback loop is demonstrated. Material formation depends on living bacterial activity and turbulent conditions, so form is not completely predefined; the system remains laboratory-bounded, with biological growth providing partial renewal rather than wider ecological exchange.

column2: Arnardottir, T.
column4: Bacterial Sculpting: Customising Biofabrication Techniques for Biomineralisation
column5: Bioprotopia: Designing the Built Environment with Living Organisms
column9: Bacterial Sculpting investigates biomineralisation as a processual fabrication strategy in which microbial activity contributes directly to material formation. Rather than treating living matter as a passive casting medium, the approach customises conditions so biological processes participate in shaping mineralised outcomes.
column19: Microbe → mineral deposition → fabricated material
column20: No operational digital feedback loop is central to the work. Microbial agency makes material outcomes process-dependent and partly emergent, but the experiments remain bounded to fabrication; renewal is present through biological production rather than through wider ecological cycles.

column2: Toffoli, T.; Margolus, N.
column4: Programmable matter: Concepts and realization
column9: Programmable matter is introduced as a computational concept in which physical substance is composed of locally programmable units capable of implementing general behaviours. The article functions as a manifesto, tutorial and call for experiments connecting computation and physical matter.
column19: Computational unit → programmable material aggregate
column20: The contribution defines a computational paradigm rather than an implemented digital–material feedback system. Behaviour is conceived as programmable within an artificial material substrate; ecological exchange, evolving relational definitions and material renewal are outside its scope.

column2: Gilpin, K.; Knaian, A.; Rus, D.
column4: Robot Pebbles: One Centimeter Modules for Programmable Matter through Self-Disassembly
column5: 2010 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
column9: A programmable-matter system is built from autonomous one-centimetre modules that bond, communicate and share power using electropermanent magnets. Distributed data and local coordination allow an initial block of modules to create two-dimensional target shapes by selectively detaching unnecessary units.
column19: Autonomous module → communicating aggregate → target shape
column20: Embedded communication and distributed computation maintain strong information exchange among physical material modules. Shape formation is nevertheless directed towards predefined targets in a bounded robotic system; detachable modules support reuse, but wider ecological exchange and replenishment are absent.

column2: Hiller, J.; Lipson, H.
column4: Design and analysis of digital materials for physical 3D voxel printing
column9: Physical voxels are proposed as discrete material building blocks for a massively parallel additive-manufacturing process in which matter is digital. Material behaviour and manufacturability are analysed through assemblies of pre-existing units rather than continuous deposition.
column19: Voxel → lattice → fabricated object
column20: Digital representation and physical discretisation are closely aligned, but no operational feedback loop updates the digital model from material behaviour. Material properties and connectivity are designed within a bounded fabrication system, without contextual exchange or renewal mechanisms.

column2: MacCurdy, R.; McNicoll, A.; Lipson, H.
column4: Bitblox: Printable digital materials for electromechanical machines
column5: The International Journal of Robotics Research, 33(10)
column9: Bitblox are modular interconnecting blocks that embed electromechanical connectivity and function. The unique combination and spatial arrangement of blocks determine the mechanical and electrical properties of an assembly, allowing electromechanical machines to be constructed from discrete material units.
column19: Functional block → assembly → electromechanical machine
column20: Physical modules contain computational/electromechanical functionality, giving partial digital–material discourse, but assembly relationships are predefined and the system remains bounded. No wider contextual exchange, evolving relationship logic, or material replenishment is implemented.

column2: Hilbertz, W. H.
column4: Electrodeposition of Minerals in Sea Water: Experiments and Applications
column9: Direct electrical current between electrodes in seawater precipitates calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide onto cathodes. Experiments demonstrate mineral accretion as a building process for marine structures and artificial reefs, using dissolved seawater constituents as the material source.
column18: Continuous mineral accretion over extended deployment
column19: Electrode → mineral accretion → marine structure / habitat
column20: Electrical input directly regulates physical mineral growth, but no sensing-based digital feedback loop is demonstrated. Material formation depends on open seawater chemistry and continues through environmental resource flows; marine-habitat applications create explicit contextual exchange and replenishment.

column2: Swackhamer, M.; Satterfield, B.; Buma, B.; Rhodes, H.; et al.
column4: Nurse Pod - A Critical Examination of the Role of Decay in Architecture
column9: Nurse Pod applies design and digital fabrication to sacrificial structures that support tree seedlings during forest recovery. Inspired by nurse logs, biodegradable vessels protect and nurture young trees, then decay so their material contributes to the developing ecological system.
column18: Seedling establishment → scaffold decay → forest recovery
column19: Fabricated pod → tree seedling → forest succession
column20: Digital design is used in fabrication rather than as a live feedback system. The architecture is intentionally temporary and embedded in forest recovery; material decay, changing ecological roles, succession and nutrient return are explicit parts of the design logic.

column2: Satterfield, B.; Swackhamer, M.
column4: Material Custodies: Embracing Loss, Failure, and Death as Opportunities in Wood Construction
column9: Wood construction is reframed as a temporary custody within a larger material and ecological lifecycle. Architectural use is treated as a fleeting sequestration between prior and future states, allowing loss, failure, decomposition and return to become design conditions rather than endpoints.
column18: Material life cycle from growth through use and return
column19: Wood resource → architecture → decay / future ecosystem
column20: No digital feedback loop is implemented. Material relationships are explicitly lifecycle-based and expected to change through use, failure and decay; architecture is situated within ecological material flows and return to future resources is central.

column2: O’Donoghue, T.; Minasny, B.; McBratney, A.
column4: Digital Regenerative Agriculture
column9: Precision, digital and smart-agriculture tools are reframed from productivity and efficiency objectives towards ecological renewal. The perspective considers how sensing, spatial data and digital assessment can quantify and guide regenerative contributions made by farmscapes.
column18: Seasonal to multi-year agricultural and soil cycles
column19: Soil / field sensing → farm management → farmscape / ecosystem
column20: Digital tools provide monitoring and decision support, creating partial feedback with physical agricultural systems rather than a single automated control loop. Regenerative management depends on changing ecological conditions and explicitly targets soil, landscape and ecosystem renewal.

column2: Liu, Z.; Li, M.; Ji, W.
column4: Development and application of a digital twin model for Net zero energy building operation and maintenance utilizing BIM-IoT integration
column9: A BIM-IoT digital twin integrates operational building data through collection, model construction, simulation, validation and automated feedback control. The system is designed to improve operation and maintenance efficiency for net-zero-energy buildings through continuous sensing and digital representation.
column19: Sensor / equipment → BIM-IoT twin → building-control system
column20: Continuous sensing and automated feedback establish strong digital–physical discourse. The twin remains focused on a defined building and performance objectives; models can update with operational data, but control relationships and optimisation goals are substantially predefined and ecological renewal is outside scope.

column2: Oxman, N.; Rosenberg, J. L.
column4: Material-based Design Computation: An Inquiry into Digital Simulation of Physical Material Properties as Design Generators
column9: Physical material properties are translated into geometrical functions so elastic membrane behaviour can become a form-generating design input. A Processing-based digital tool simulates material behaviour and predicts deformation under specified environmental conditions.
column19: Material property → digital simulation → geometric form
column20: Material behaviour informs computation, but the physical artefact does not maintain an operational feedback relationship with the digital representation. Simulation assumes defined material and environmental conditions; wider context, evolving relations and renewal are not addressed.

column2: Oxman, N.
column4: Structuring Materiality: Design Fabrication of Heterogeneous Materials
column9: Variable Property Design treats materiality as a generative design driver by modelling, simulating and fabricating assemblies with spatially varying properties. Material distributions are configured to respond to multiple and continuously shifting functional constraints through heterogeneous fabrication.
column19: Functional constraints → variable property model → heterogeneous material
column20: Digital computation varies material properties in response to multiple design constraints, but the fabricated material does not update the digital model during operation. Constraint relationships can change during design, while the final material system remains bounded and does not include ecological exchange or renewal.

column2: Oxman, N.; Laucks, J.; Kayser, M.; Duro-Royo, J.; Gonzalez Uribe, C. D.
column4: Silk Pavilion: A Case Study in Fiber-based Digital Fabrication
column9: The Silk Pavilion combines computational fibre placement with biological fabrication by silkworms. Algorithmic thread-density gradients respond to environmental constraints, while thousands of silkworms deposit secondary fibres across a CNC-fabricated scaffold, linking digital geometry, material behaviour and biological production.
column18: Digital scaffold fabrication followed by biological deposition
column19: Environmental constraints → computational scaffold → silkworm deposition → pavilion
column20: Digital design establishes a scaffold and environmental conditions that influence biological fabrication, creating partial digital–biological discourse without continuous feedback from the living process to the model. Biological agency and environmental factors affect material formation, but the system remains a designed pavilion rather than a wider ecological exchange network.

column2: Crawford, A.; In-na, P.; Caldwell, G.; Armstrong, R.; Bridgens, B.
column4: Clay 3D printing as a bio-design research tool: development of photosynthetic living building components
column8: Clay additive manufacturing is used to develop living building components that support photosynthetic microalgae. Digital fabrication controls geometry and material porosity while biological experiments assess how the resulting ceramic substrates can maintain living photosynthetic activity.
column9: Adam Blaney
column18: Fabrication followed by sustained biological activity
column19: Digital geometry → clay substrate → microalgae / photosynthetic component
column20: Digital fabrication shapes the habitat but no live digital feedback loop responds to organism behaviour. Biological performance depends on substrate and environmental conditions, giving partial adaptability and contextual relation; living activity provides limited renewal without a broader ecological material cycle.

column2: Ilgun, A.; Angelov, K.; Stefanec, M.; Schönwetter-Fuchs, S.; et al.
column4: Bio-Hybrid Systems for Ecosystem Level Effects
column5: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Artificial Life
column9: HIVEOPOLIS is presented as a bio-hybrid system linking computational, robotic and biological processes around honeybee colonies. Robotic devices and sensing are considered as means to interact with colony behaviour and extend intervention from individual hives toward ecosystem-level effects.
column18: Continuous colony behaviour and seasonal ecological cycles
column19: Robotic/computational system ↔ bee colony → surrounding ecosystem
column20: Bio-hybrid robotics and sensing establish strong digital–biological feedback, while bee behaviour and ecological conditions remain dynamic rather than fixed. The system is explicitly positioned toward ecosystem-level effects; renewal is present through biological/ecological processes but material return is not its primary focus.

column2: Parker, D.; Ilgun, Z. A.; Lim, A. C. S.; Vasatko, H.; Vu, D. V.; Piórecka, N.; Keune, S.
column4: I.N.S.E.C.T. Wall Twin: Designing for and with Insects, Fungi, and Humans
column9: An architectural installation is developed to support coexistence among local insects, fungi and humans. Bio-digital manufacturing, mycelium, textiles and 3D printing are combined with interspecies design methods that recognise nonhuman stakeholders and habitat relations as part of the design process.
column19: Fabricated habitat → fungi/insects/humans → local ecological relations
column20: Digital fabrication is used to construct the habitat but no live digital feedback loop is central. The artefact is explicitly situated within multispecies relations whose participants and interactions can change; ecological context is central, while renewal and material return are present only partially.

column2: Sicher, E.
column4: “How can SCOBY be grown from scratch?”: Growing materials from situated ecologies
column9: SCOBY cultivation is reframed from reliance on standardised cultures toward material growth emerging from situated plants, microbes and vernacular fermentation practices. Fieldwork in Thailand and Germany informs an open-source method and a Situated Growing Design approach grounded in bioregional ecological relationships.
column18: Fermentation, cultivation and bioregional material cycles
column19: Local plants/microbes → SCOBY growth → situated material practice / bioregion
column20: No digital feedback system is implemented. Material formation depends explicitly on situated ecological relations, microbial adaptation and local resource conditions; relationships are expected to vary with context, and regeneration, provenance and bioregional renewal are central.

column2: Mitterberger, D.; Derme, T.
column4: Digital soil: Robotically 3D-printed granular bio-composites
column9: A robotic additive-manufacturing framework uses organic granular soil-based composites as an alternative to homogeneous, non-biodegradable fabrication materials. The work treats soil's volatility and environmental sensitivity as design parameters and investigates water-based robotic deposition for biodegradable structures.
column18: Robotic fabrication followed by environmental/material change
column19: Organic granular material → robotic deposition → biodegradable structure / environment
column20: Robotic fabrication is computationally controlled but no live material-to-digital feedback loop is demonstrated. Soil variability and environmental factors are acknowledged as active design conditions; biodegradability provides partial lifecycle return, while wider ecological exchange remains limited.

column2: Derme, T.; Mitterberger, D.
column4: The Synchronous Garden (SynG): New Perspectives between Architecture and Ecology
column5: Nonlinear Urbanism: Towards Multiple Urban Futures
column9: The Synchronous Garden reframes architecture and ecology as dynamic, technologically mediated relations rather than separate or static domains. Living materials, signals, multiple scales and temporalities are used to consider architecture as capable of continual adaptation, evolution, change and finite lifespans.
column18: Continuous adaptation across biological and architectural timescales
column19: Signals / living materials → architectural environment → ecological relations
column20: Digital and sensing technologies are positioned as mediators of living architectural processes rather than as a single demonstrated control loop. Relationships are explicitly dynamic and temporally variable, with architecture situated within ecological relations; material return and replenishment are acknowledged but not developed as a complete cycle.

column2: Derme, T.; Mitterberger, D.
column4: Sylva: An Autonomous Hydroponic Garden Cared for by Two Robots
column9: Sylva is an autonomous hydroponic garden maintained by two robots that water, distribute seeds and monitor plant growth. External data, data prediction and real-time interactions influence the geometry and development of the garden, combining botany, computer vision, robotics and architectural design.
column18: Continuous robotic maintenance and plant growth
column19: Data / robots ↔ hydroponic plants → constructed garden
column20: Monitoring and robotic care create strong digital–physical/biological feedback. Plant growth and data update system operation, but the garden remains a designed indoor habitat with bounded resources; ecological context and renewal are present through living growth rather than open material exchange.

column2: Derme, T.; Battal, A.; Boscoboinik, N.; Schwarze, F. W. M. R.; Dillenburger, B.
column4: Braided mycelium composites: an integrated robotic design-to-fabrication method for bio-based fibrous building components
column9: An integrated robotic workflow combines braided fibrous reinforcement with mycelium-based composites to produce customised bio-based building components. Computational design and robotic fabrication address continuity, repeatability and scaling while retaining biological growth as part of material production.
column19: Computational design → braided reinforcement → mycelium growth → component
column20: Digital design and robotic fabrication are tightly integrated with biological material production, but the living process does not continuously update the digital model. Growth introduces material variability and partial renewal within a bounded fabrication system; wider ecological exchange is not central.
